section_map.summary: The abstract compresses the management objective, one-dimensional cellular representation, visitor-object rules, daily adaptation, satisfaction criteria, and the headline 1102-capacity result into one forward-moving paragraph.

The introduction moves from growth in rafting participation to encounter norms and prior wilderness simulation, identifies the inflexibility of static itineraries, and motivates a demand-responsive dynamic scheduler.
The plan of attack restates the 225-mile, Y-campsite, six-to-eighteen-day decision and previews assumptions, criteria, a cellular model, implementation variants, evaluation, and capacity selection.

The assumptions translate craft speeds, daily rafting hours, uniform campsites, local visitor activity, maintenance, constant mean arrivals, and advance booking into a daily discrete scheduling surface.

The definitions distinguish three encounter types, schedule deviation, rejected demand, absolute capacity, practical carrying capacity, satisfaction constraints, flexibility, robustness, and implementability.

The comparison first credits static schedules for conflict-free predictability, then names their demand and throughput costs and replaces them with a rolling day-by-day destination assignment that can be planned in advance.

The core section defines the river array, Poisson loading, visitor state, ideal movement, bump priority, conflict resolution, completion calculations, seven implementations, interaction geometry, rejection sets, and satisfaction metrics.
The results compare implementation variants, then sweep Y and lambda through interaction, rejection, off-schedule, and completion surfaces before selecting maximum and economic capacity points.

The extension breaks the fixed-campsite and uninterrupted-flow assumptions, removes campsites through an environmental-degradation rule, pauses movement and loading during Poisson-duration storms, and maps operational responses.

The conclusion reconnects customer-choice flexibility, conflict elimination, satisfaction metrics, the 1102 maximum, the 1074 practical point, adverse-event tests, and claimed transfer to other one-dimensional rivers.

The memo translates the cellular scheduler into advance-booking, daily placement, conflict reassignment, capacity, on-time completion, interaction, storm, environmental, and scale-up claims for rafting managers.

Ten notes supply recreation-demand, social-norm, wilderness-simulation, safety, itinerary, parks, encounter-norm, and cellular-automaton context while leaving code, seeds, raw runs, and complete task text absent.

assumptions.summary: Oar and motor rafts operate within the Table 1 speed ranges for four to eight hours per day.
Daily motion depends on initial and final campsite positions rather than within-day speed variation.
Y campsites are equivalent, uniformly distributed, maintained, and available unless a later stress test removes them.
Campsites are offset from the river and visitor activity remains local to the assigned site.
The mean number of visitors entering per day is constant and represented by lambda.
Visitors make reservations at least twenty-four hours in advance.
The dynamic scheduler has access to current visitors and next-day arrivals when assigning destinations.
The river can be represented as a one-dimensional cellular array updated once per day.
Rejected demand, off-schedule completion, and encounter rates are sufficient customer-satisfaction proxies.
Environmental degradation and storm interruption can be represented through campsite removal and paused daily transitions.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The paper restates a 225-mile river, Y campsites, six-to-eighteen-day trips, and oar or motor propulsion.
Table 1 gives both craft types a three-mph minimum, maxima of five and ten mph, and four-to-eight-hour rafting days.
Daily load follows a Poisson process with parameter lambda in the flow diagram.
Table 3 defines seven implementation rule combinations A-G.
Tables 4 and 5 report visitor totals, rejection, interactions, and timing for selected implementations.
Figure 5 sweeps Y and lambda for average boat interactions.
Figure 6 sweeps Y and lambda for rejected visitors.
Figure 7 sweeps Y and lambda for off-schedule completion with contour levels 54 through 0.
Figure 8 sweeps Y and lambda for completed visitors with contour levels 1000 through 200.
Table 6 uses Y=110 and alpha rows zero, ten, twenty, and thirty, but omits the four lambda column values.
Storm tests use Y=110, four lambda values, four occurrence probabilities, and mean duration mu equal to one day, but the table of results is not printed.

results_trace.summary: Implementation A completes 756 visitors with 3.8 percent rejection and 2.1 percent off-schedule in Table 4.
Removing optimal movement in implementation B raises off-schedule completion to 42.3 percent in Table 4.
Implementation A reports 7.10 interactions per visitor and 2.2 percent off-schedule in Table 5.
Upstream bumping in implementation F reduces interactions but rejects 35.0 percent of requests.
Interaction surfaces remain below about ten over the displayed grid and decline with added campsites.
Rejection falls sharply with Y and rises with lambda when campsites are scarce.
Off-schedule completion approaches zero as Y increases in the displayed grid.
The claimed maximum is 1102 visitors or groups at Y=180 and lambda=15.
At the claimed maximum, rejection is 1.79 percent, off-schedule completion is 0.67 percent, and interactions are 10.35 per person per season.
A lower-resource point at Y=100 and lambda=15 is reported to complete 1025 visitor groups.
Large alpha values substantially reduce visitor totals and increase rejection and off-schedule percentages in Table 6.
The conclusion reports a practical point of 1074 visitors at Y=110 and lambda=15 under a visitors-to-campsites ratio criterion.

weaknesses.summary: The title page retains the template word Subtitle and the abstract contains subject-verb and wording defects; these are source defects, not extraction omissions.
The abstract says 1102 visitors although the simulated objects and later economic paragraph sometimes refer to visitor groups; the unit must remain typed.
Pages 2 through 23 visibly overlap C.A.R.S with Cellular Automaton Rafting Simulation in the footer.
No official problem statement was found locally; task reconstruction relies on the paper's own restatement and remains incomplete.
Uniform equivalent campsites, constant mean daily arrivals, advance booking, and routine maintenance exclude important spatial, seasonal, labor, and closure variation.
Absolute capacity 180Y counts one visitor group per campsite-day without trip-duration occupancy, interaction, launch, exit, or satisfaction constraints.
The dynamic strategy promises conflict elimination but the algorithm later describes resolving occupied cells rather than proving global conflict-free feasibility.
The paper says the dynamic model can be planned in advance but does not specify the optimization horizon, forecast update, rollback, or computational complexity.
The bump coefficient beta and ideal movement y-star are displayed as the same ratio despite serving priority and movement roles.
The conflict step says cells with more than two visitors, apparently omitting the exactly-two case that should already violate one-group campsite capacity.
Bump direction reversal is mentioned, but tie handling, boundary handling, repeated collision resolution, and termination are not formalized.
Poisson loading lacks a seed, repeated-run count, warm-up, confidence interval, and explicit mapping from arrivals to individual trip requests.
The seven implementation variants do not report matched random streams or replication uncertainty, limiting causal claims from Tables 4 and 5.
The carrying-capacity definition uses fewer than ten interactions per person per day, while the final result reports interactions per person per season.
The source says one rafting reason where season is intended, and its encounter metric omits raft-to-camp and camp-to-camp measures defined earlier.
Table 5 implementation G duplicates the visitor and percentage pattern of Table 4 implementation D, which may be a copied row but is visually present in the source.
Tables 4 and 5 provide single point estimates without seeds, run counts, variance, intervals, or raw outputs.
Figure 5 alternates among interactions per tourist, per trip, per visitor, per person, per day, and per season without one invariant denominator.
The argument compares a ten-interactions-per-day standard with fewer than ten total interactions over a season, a dimensional mismatch.
The claim that off-schedule completion becomes independent of lambda at large Y is visual and has no fitted model, uncertainty band, or tested-domain boundary.
The result alternates between 1102 and 1102.8 without an explicit rounding rule.
The maximum capacity is reported at Y=180 and lambda=15, but no proof shows it is the global optimum outside the displayed grid.
The body practical alternative is 1025 groups at Y=100, lambda=15, while the conclusion gives 1074 visitors at Y=110, lambda=15 under a different ratio criterion.
The environmental formula prints square brackets but does not define rounding, nonnegativity, time indexing, recovery, cumulative use, or the base of the logarithm.
Table 6 omits the four lambda column values, so its numeric columns cannot be independently interpreted.
The storm sentence displays no comparison sign before 5 percent; a targeted crop confirms the character is absent rather than corrupted.
Storm occurrence probability, independence, event overlap, duration truncation, and the meaning of incrementing D_i are not fully specified.
The conclusion displays Y ¿ 110; the source PDF has a broken greater-than glyph and must not be silently normalized without warning.
Claims of strong real-world performance and transfer to any one-dimensional rafting system exceed the limited synthetic scenarios and absent field calibration.
The memo extrapolates from one 225-mile river to thousands of visitors on several longer rivers without modeling network topology or shared resources.
Reference URLs display inverted punctuation instead of angle brackets, and no code, seeds, raw schedules, or machine-readable results are supplied.
Several references are incomplete or inconsistently formatted, limiting provenance and reproducibility checks.

independent_extensions.summary: Define an exact conflict-resolution loop for two or more visitors, including beta ties, boundaries, repeated bumps, cycle detection, and termination.
Publish pseudocode or executable code with fixed seeds, typed visitor requests, state invariants, and machine-readable outputs.
Choose one interaction denominator and retain raft-to-raft, raft-to-camp, and camp-to-camp measures separately.
Use common random numbers and repeated runs for A-G with intervals and paired mechanism-effect estimates.
Construct a Pareto frontier over completed groups, rejection, delay, interactions, campsite count, and maintenance cost rather than one capacity scalar.
Search a declared Y-lambda domain with exact constraints or bounded optimization and publish the full feasible set.
Model campsite degradation as cumulative state with recovery, heterogeneity, closure duration, and empirically calibrated use effects.
Use an explicit storm arrival process, duration law, overlap rule, travel-safety state, and customer-notification policy.
Calibrate demand, group size, spatial geometry, craft speed, closures, encounter tolerance, safety, staffing, and multi-river topology before transfer.
Generate the memo from a typed result object so rounding, capacity, practical point, interaction units, and uncertainty cannot drift.
